explanation.surface: A notice announcing a strike is being handed round.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is the cry that calls workers off the job: 'hands' are workers, and 'out' means on strike.
explanation.definitionFit: To give things round to a group is to deal them out by hand; and a call for labourers to down tools would be phrased as workers leaving.

clue.text: Court gets rough with bad kidnapper

indicators.note: rough suggests something handled crudely and knocked out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A judge's court comes down hard on a wicked kidnapper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rough' signals rearranging the letters of COURT and BAD together; 'gets' and 'with' only join the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Abduction is the crime of taking someone away by force, so one who commits it is a kidnapper.

parts.note: bottle here is slang for nerve, so this is the nerve that comes from drinking rather than a container of alcohol

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottle' is British slang for courage or nerve; the phrase is bravery found in drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names the false bravery a person gains after drinking alcohol, bottle being slang for nerve.

clue.text: Lines up a ship in port

parts.note: a poem is a set of lines, and an ode is a kind of poem

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the following words are read from the bottom, so they come out backwards

parts.note: SS is the abbreviation for steamship

explanation.surface: Ships queue in a line to enter a harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' sits between the pieces and turns 'a ship' as one unit, as it would read climbing a down column; 'Lines' looks like a queue but is poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: Odessa is a major Black Sea harbour city in Ukraine, so it is an example of a seaport.

explanation.surface: A swindler's scheme ends up causing bother.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'do' someone is British slang for cheating them, so a con artist's goal is to do you; a to-do is a fuss.
explanation.definitionFit: A swindler sets out to cheat his mark, slang 'do'; and a commotion or fuss is called a to-do.

clue.text: All is not as it should be in the stud

indicators.note: the letters are not yet in proper order, and setting them as they should be rearranges them into the right word

explanation.surface: Something is amiss at the horse-breeding farm.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is ALL IS NOT; 'as it should be' asks for those letters to be set right, giving a horse kept in the stud.
explanation.definitionFit: A stud is a male horse kept for breeding, which is exactly what an uncastrated male horse is used for.

clue.text: One gentile rose to see a Hindu ascetic

indicators.note: in a down clue, rose means the pieces climb upwards, so they read in reverse

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
goy is a Yiddish word for a gentile, a non-Jew

explanation.surface: A non-Jewish man got up to visit an Indian holy man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rose' reverses I plus GOY together; GOY is Yiddish for a non-Jew.
explanation.definitionFit: A yogi is a practitioner of yoga, typically a Hindu holy man who practises self-denial.

clue.text: One who lays about the boat crew in build up

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, so the bird wraps round the rowing crew

parts.note: a hen is a bird that lays eggs
an eight is a rowing crew of eight oarsmen

explanation.surface: A bricklayer is working on the boat crew as they bulk up.
explanation.walkthrough: An 'eight' is a racing rowing crew; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To intensify or increase something is to raise it higher, to build it up.

parts.note: a shoe-shiner would make boots gleam, so a better polisher literally beat others at shining

explanation.walkthrough: A boot-black is a shoe-shiner; the word for surpassing others is read literally as shining more.
explanation.definitionFit: To surpass others is to shine brighter than them, which is literally what a good shoe-polisher does.

clue.text: Prepare to put out with the turn of the tide

indicators.note: the turn of the tide suggests something going back the other way, so the word is read in reverse

explanation.surface: Getting ready to sail out as the tide changes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' suggests a boat leaving harbour, but here it means publish.
explanation.definitionFit: Editing is getting a text ready for publication, that is, preparing it to be issued.

parts.note: existing is read as staying alive, so these are what it costs to keep going day to day

explanation.walkthrough: 'Existing' looks like an adjective (current expenses) but means simply being alive.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means the general price of everyday necessities like food and housing, the outlay of staying alive.

indicators.note: bursts suggests the letters breaking apart and scattering, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Insults are hurled when the private row spills into the open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bursts' signals rearranging all the letters of OUT IN PRIVATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Vituperation is bitter, abusive language: a torrent of insults.

parts.note: stakes and raised hint at gambling bets, but these are wooden posts set upright to protect a place

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stakes raised' reads like upping a bet; it means wooden posts put up as a barrier.
explanation.definitionFit: A stockade is a defensive enclosure built of upright wooden posts driven into the ground.

clue.text: It's all over a point in the revised deed

indicators.note: in places the compass letter inside the rearranged letters
revised means changed or reworked, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: N is a point of the compass, north

explanation.surface: Once a point in the amended deed is settled, the matter is closed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revised' rearranges DEED into EDED, and 'in' puts N inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that is finished or concluded has come to a close: it is all over.
As an adjective it means firmly resolved or determined; as a noun it means an aim or plan.

clue.text: Father to the French, married to the Germans

parts.note: Fr is the abbreviation for Father, a priest's title
au is French for 'to the' before a masculine noun

explanation.surface: A priest is French, but his wife is German.
explanation.walkthrough: In German, a Frau is a wife or married woman, the title Mrs.
explanation.definitionFit: The German word is used for a wife or married woman, the equivalent of Mrs.

indicators.note: occupied by means the businesses have the listening organ living inside them

parts.note: firms are business companies
the ear is the organ that receives sound

explanation.surface: Arms companies are being taken over by a receiver.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'receiver' sounds like an official who takes over a bankrupt company; here it is the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: Guns and rifles together make up a collection of weapons.

explanation.surface: A seat in an American bar.
explanation.walkthrough: A saloon is the British word for a closed family car; in the US it is called a sedan. A sedan chair is an enclosed seat carried on poles.
explanation.definitionFit: The first is the enclosed seat carried by bearers on poles; the second is the US word for a closed four-door car.

clue.text: Drug could have bearing on the case

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed above, so the compass bearing comes first

parts.note: SE, south-east, is a compass bearing
the dative is a grammatical case in Latin and German

explanation.surface: A drug might affect the outcome of a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' suggests a trial but is a grammar case; 'on' puts SE above it in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A calming medicine that soothes or makes one sleepy is a type of drug.

clue.text: Father is not out to cause distress

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father
a batsman who is not out in cricket is still in

explanation.surface: Dad stays at home so as to upset someone.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a batsman who is 'not out' is still in.
explanation.definitionFit: To hurt or upset someone is to cause them suffering, as grief does.

clue.text: Building Elsie and Ida regard as perfect

indicators.note: building suggests constructing something new, so these letters are put together in a fresh order

explanation.surface: Two women think their new building is flawless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Building' signals rearranging the letters of ELSIE and IDA together; 'and' joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: To idealise someone is to see them as flawless, without faults.
As a verb it means to look at or consider; as a noun it means respect or high opinion.

explanation.surface: Someone set off behind schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'late' reads as tardy, but here means dead, as in 'the late Mr Smith'.
explanation.definitionFit: Setting off on a journey is leaving; and the dead are euphemistically said to have gone or passed on.

parts.note: pig iron is crude iron from a blast furnace
an eon is a very long age

explanation.surface: A kind of bird from the Iron Age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iron age' looks like the prehistoric period, but splits into pig iron and an eon.
explanation.definitionFit: A pigeon is a common plump grey bird, a kind of dove.

clue.text: It occurs to one later that this is the time to

definitions.text: It occurs to one later that this is the time to

parts.words: It occurs to one later that this is the time to
parts.note: an idea that comes late, and its two halves name the moment it arrives, after thinking

explanation.walkthrough: The clue stops short on 'to', as if the thought came too late to finish it; the answer splits into the time an idea comes and the idea itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A late addition or idea that comes to mind once the main business has been done.

parts.note: sea-power suggests a naval nation, but this is the force the moon exerts on ocean waters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sea-power' suggests a naval nation like Britain; it means the force that moves the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: The regular rise and fall of the ocean is a mighty natural force of the sea.

indicators.note: going round means the ring and road surround the next letter

parts.note: a ring is round, the shape of the letter O
St is the abbreviation for street, a road

explanation.surface: A ring road loops round a building for drying hops.
explanation.walkthrough: An oast is a kiln for drying hops in Kent; 'Ring-road' splits into O and ST.
explanation.definitionFit: An oast is a kiln, often with a conical roof, for drying hops for beer.

clue.text: Knight I sent back for the flag

indicators.note: sent back means the title is turned around and read backwards

parts.note: Sir is the title given to a knight

explanation.surface: A knight returns a banner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag' is not a banner but the yellow flag iris, a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The flag is a name for a type of wild iris, a plant with sword-shaped leaves.

parts.note: deliveries suggests couriers, but here it means delivering babies in childbirth

explanation.walkthrough: 'Deliveries' sounds like parcels; it is births, delivered in person.
explanation.definitionFit: These nurses assist women in childbirth, delivering babies.

clue.text: Was in occupation, with mind to become a stake-holder

indicators.note: holder means the first word holds the second, so the minding verb contains the betting stake

parts.note: to mind is to tend, look after
an ante is a stake put up in poker

explanation.surface: Someone living somewhere intends to buy a share in the business.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated 'stake-holder' splits in two: 'holder' is the container signal and 'stake' its contents; 'with' and 'to become a' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who rented and lived in a property occupied it as a resident.
